probes.query: I discarded a long stretch of old operation history and then ran the storage-cleanup command with its expiry set to the present moment. Trace how commits that only the discarded history referenced end up deleted from the underlying Git store. Cover: how the discard step changes the stored history so that the commit index forgets those commits, which operation and view records the cleanup keeps, how the set of surviving commits is derived and pinned against Git's own pruning, and how Git's pruning is finally run and with what cutoff.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The discard step (cmd_op_abandon) calls op_walk::reparent_range, which writes copies of every descendant operation with rewritten parent lists (attached to the destination operation), so those operations get new operation IDs and the old ones become unreachable.

CRITICAL: The default index store keys its saved index by operation ID (op_links directory). The new head operation has no saved link, so get_index_at_op falls back to build_index_at_operation, which starts from the nearest ancestor operation that has a link (for example the root operation) and indexes only commits referenced by the surviving operations, so commits referenced only by discarded operations are never re-indexed.

build_index_at_operation collects heads from Operation::all_referenced_commit_ids (which includes the predecessor commits recorded by the operation) plus each operation's View::all_referenced_commit_ids.

The cleanup command (cmd_util_gc) requires the head operation, uses a two-week cutoff by default (only the value 'now' is accepted to override), and calls the operation store's gc with the current operation as the only head, then GitBackend::gc with the current index.

SimpleOpStore::gc walks operations depth-first from the head to find reachable operations and their views, then deletes operation and view files that are not reachable unless their modification time is newer than the cutoff.

GitBackend::gc takes index.all_heads_for_gc() (heads of all indexed commits, excluding the root commit), rewrites the refs under refs/jj/keep/<commit id> via recreate_no_gc_refs (deleting other keep refs unless the loose ref is newer than the cutoff), garbage-collects the extra-metadata table segments, and then runs git gc through the configured Git executable with a prune cutoff of the form @<unix seconds> +0000.

probes.query: I have several unrelated fixes sitting in my working-copy commit, and each touches lines that were last changed in a different earlier commit of my stack. I want jj to push every fix back into the commit where its lines were last modified, automatically. How does it decide which earlier commits are eligible by default, how does it work out which commit each changed line belongs to (and how is the per-file history lookup kept cheap), which kinds of changes does it refuse or leave behind, how is a moved change combined with the receiving commit, and under what condition does my original commit disappear afterwards?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: By default the receiving commits are the mutable ones: the destination argument defaults to the mutable() revset, defined in revsets.toml as ~immutable(), where immutable() is ::(immutable_heads() | root()); only ancestors of the source are considered, and the chosen targets are checked with check_rewritable.

CRITICAL: split_hunks_to_trees annotates the parent-side text of each changed file (FileAnnotator::with_file_content, computed with the destinations as the domain); annotate::process_commits builds the revset heads | (domain & ancestors(heads)) filtered by the File predicate for that path, walks the graph, and propagates line identity to parents through a line diff (copy_same_lines_with using ContentDiff::by_line). Lines with unresolved origin are dropped when annotation ranges are built.

The File predicate in the default revset engine uses the changed-path index (index.changed_paths()) when the commit is covered, and otherwise falls back to diffing the commit against its parents (has_diff_from_parent) with the file matcher.

split_file_hunks moves a modification or insertion only if its left range lies wholly inside one annotation range, and treats a pure insertion exactly between two annotation ranges as ambiguous (left behind); a pure deletion may span several contiguous annotation ranges and is split among them.

Paths that are new files are skipped silently; symlinks, conflicted files, Git submodules and access-denied files are reported as skipped with a reason (to_file_value); a file deletion is propagated only for a destination whose selected hunks delete the entire file content.

absorb_hunks runs transform_descendants: each receiving commit is rebased and its tree becomes a three-way MergedTree::merge of (its tree, the source's parent tree, the tree with the selected hunks) with absorb-specific labels, and the source commit is added to its predecessors; the source commit is reparented (hunks removed) and abandoned only if is_discardable() (no changes left and an empty description).

probes.query: I turned on commit signing in my configuration but never run any dedicated signing command. Trace how a commit that jj writes or rewrites ends up carrying a cryptographic signature inside the Git object. Cover: which rule decides whether a given commit gets signed (and how that changes when someone else authored it or it was already signed), how the signing program is chosen among the supported ones, how the signing key is picked when none is given for the GPG family versus SSH, where in the Git commit the signature is stored, and how pushing treats commits that are not signed yet.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: SignSettings::should_sign (settings.rs) decides per commit from the configured behavior: drop never signs; keep signs only if the commit already has a signature and its author email equals the user email; own signs whenever the author email equals the user email; force always signs. The default behavior is keep and the default backend is none (lib/src/config/misc.toml).

CRITICAL: commit_builder::write_to_store signs only if store.signer().can_sign() (a main backend is configured) and should_sign is true; it clears the commit's old secure_sig and passes a signing closure (Signer::sign with an optional per-commit key override) into Store::write_commit.

The Signer is built when the repo loader is initialized from the file system (RepoLoader::init_from_file_system in repo.rs calls signing_factory::signer_from_settings): it instantiates the GPG, GPGSM and SSH backends (plus a test one), picks the main backend by the configured backend name (none means no main backend, an unknown name is an error), and keeps the others only for verification.

Default key when no override is given: GPG uses the configured signing key, falling back to the user email; GPGSM always falls back to the user email; SSH uses the configured signing key and returns a MissingKey error if there is none.

GitBackend::write_commit serializes the commit, calls the signing closure on those bytes, and stores the signature as an extra commit header whose name depends on the Git hash kind (signature_field_name), and keeps the signed data in the commit's secure signature.

On push, when the sign-on-push setting is on (default false), sign_commits_before_push forces the 'own' behavior, signs only mutable unsigned commits authored by the user (reparenting descendants and remapping the pushed ref updates), and warns about immutable commits that need a signature but are skipped.

probes.query: When I divide a commit by choosing changes in an external graphical program that I named in my configuration, how does jj hand that program the before and after content and take the edited result back? Cover: how the configured name becomes a program plus argument list (and what happens when the name is not a configured tool, or no editor is configured at all), what decides whether the program is shown two folders or three, which files are placed on disk and which sides are made read-only, where the instruction text for the user goes and when it is removed, how a tool that has to be started once per file differs, and how the edited folder becomes the new tree.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DiffEditor::from_settings reads the editor setting (ui.diff-editor) through editor_args_from_settings; if it is unset it prints a hint and uses the builtin editor. A string value that names a built-in or a [merge-tools.<name>] entry is resolved via DiffEditTool::get_tool_config / get_external_tool_config (program defaults to the tool name); otherwise the value is treated as a literal command line, split into a program and arguments (ExternalMergeTool::with_edit_args; with no arguments the default left/right arguments apply). An explicitly requested tool name that is not configured is run as a program of that name with default arguments. An external tool whose edit arguments are empty is rejected.

CRITICAL: edit_diff_external decides two-way versus three-way by scanning the edit arguments for an output variable (find_all_variables): present means the tool gets left, right and an editable output folder (DiffType::ThreeWay), absent means only left and right with the right folder being edited. Arguments are expanded with interpolate_variables.

check_out_trees checks out the before and after trees into temporary directories (with a state directory each) using a sparse pattern that contains only the changed files matching the matcher; the left side is made read-only, and in the three-way case the right side is read-only too.

DiffEditWorkingCopies::check_out writes the instruction text to a JJ-INSTRUCTIONS file in the editable folder (output, or right in the two-way case) only if the instructions setting is on and no such file already exists; snapshot_results deletes that file before snapshotting.

The ExternalMergeTool default edit invocation mode is Dir (one run with folder variables); with FileByFile the tool is started once for each checked-out file with per-file variables (working_copies.checked_out_files()).

snapshot_results snapshots the editable folder's tree state (output if present, else right) with an everything matcher and no size limit, and its current tree is returned as the edited tree; DiffSelector::select first restores the selected changes and skips the editor with a warning if the diff is empty.

probes.query: A local bookmark follows a branch on a remote only once that remote branch is marked as tracked. Apart from running the explicit command that starts tracking, in which situations does jj mark a remote branch as tracked by itself? Name each situation, the setting (if there is one) that controls it, and the function that makes the decision.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: When Git refs are imported (fetch, import, colocated sync), a remote bookmark seen for the first time starts tracked only if its remote is the internal local-Git pseudo-remote or its name matches that remote's configured auto-track matcher, otherwise it starts untracked; tags always start tracked. This is default_remote_ref_state_for (lib/git.rs), fed by GitImportOptions.remote_auto_track_bookmarks, which load_git_import_options builds with parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map from the per-remote settings (RemoteSettings).

CRITICAL: Creating a bookmark, or setting one that is new, starts tracking it on every remote whose matcher matches its name, where the matcher is the union of the auto-track-bookmarks and auto-track-created-bookmarks expressions (parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map_for_new_bookmarks) and tracking uses MutableRepo::track_remote_bookmark; a warning is printed if the bookmark already exists on that remote.

When cloning, the remote's default branch is tracked, but only if the chosen working branch is the default branch and the Git setting for tracking the default bookmark on clone is on (default true in misc.toml).
Exporting local bookmarks to Git records them in the view as tracked entries of the internal Git pseudo-remote (copy_exportable_local_bookmarks_to_remote_view in lib/git.rs).
After a successful push, push_refs records each pushed bookmark and tag in the remote view with state Tracked.

Renaming a bookmark carries tracking over: for each remote where the old bookmark was tracked, the new name is tracked, unless an untracked remote bookmark with the new name already exists (a warning is printed and tracking is dropped).

probes.query: Besides the commands whose job is to hide commits, in what situations does jj on its own remove a commit from visible history? I mean side effects of moving the working copy away from a commit, of picking up changes made through Git, and of reconciling concurrent operations. For each situation, name the function that decides it and the exact condition, and say where the controlling setting (if any) gets its default and how it reaches the decision.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: When the working copy leaves a commit (MutableRepo::edit and check_out), maybe_abandon_wc_commit abandons the old working-copy commit only if Commit::is_discardable (no changes relative to its parents and an empty description), no other workspace's working copy, local bookmark or local tag points at it, and it is a visible head.

CRITICAL: On Git ref import, import_refs_inner calls abandon_unreachable_commits only when the abandon-unreachable setting is on and some previously imported heads existed; it hides visible commits that were reachable from the old referenced heads but are not pinned by local bookmarks/tags, untracked visible remote refs, or the root.
The abandon-unreachable setting defaults to true in lib/src/config/misc.toml, is read into GitSettings (lib/git.rs) and reaches the import through load_git_import_options in cli/src/git_util.rs.
Commits that the import identifies as rewritten (through synthetic predecessors based on change ID) are removed from the abandoned list afterwards (abandoned_commits.retain).

When concurrent operations are merged (RepoLoader::merge_operations, triggered on divergent operation heads), MutableRepo::merge_view calls record_rewrites for the heads removed on each side, but only when the repo is backed by the default index; a removed commit whose change ID has no new visible commit is recorded as abandoned, one new commit makes it a plain rewrite, several make it a divergent rewrite.
With a non-default index, merge_view just removes the base heads that the other side dropped, with no abandon or rewrite bookkeeping.

probes.query: When I ask for a diff, or for a log with patches, what decides which output format I get? Explain the interplay of: several format options given together; an option that names an external program or a built-in format; no option at all; the configured default (which can be a built-in format name, the name of a configured external tool, or a literal command line); and how default values for context lines and for word-level alternation are layered with command-line values. Say which combinations are errors.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DiffFormatArgs places the short formats (summary, stat, types, name-only) in one mutually exclusive clap group and the long formats (git, color-words) in another, so at most one of each can be requested; diff_formats_for returns the requested formats, and only if none was requested does it fall back to default_diff_format.

CRITICAL: The tool option (diff_formats_from_args) accepts either ':<builtin>' (placed in the short or long slot by kind) or an external tool name; an external tool always occupies the long slot, and it is an error (ensure_new) if that slot, or the same builtin's slot, was already requested by another option.

default_diff_format reads the configured default (ui.diff-formatter, default ':color-words'): a string starting with ':' must be a builtin name (else a config type error); another string is looked up as a configured tool (diff_formatter_tool, which errors if the tool has no diff arguments, i.e. cannot be used for diff formatting); a string that is not a configured tool or any non-string value (a command array) is used as a literal command via ExternalMergeTool::with_diff_args.

For log-like commands (diff_formats_for_log) the list may be empty; the patch option adds the default format as the long format when none was requested, unless the requested short format equals that default.

Each builtin format takes its defaults from settings (diff.color-words.context/max-inline-alternation/conflict, diff.git.context/show-path-prefix) and then merge_args overrides context and whitespace-ignore options from the command line; the max-inline-alternation value -1 means unlimited and other negative values are a type error.

probes.query: I wrote a command alias inside a config block that applies only to one subcommand, and another alias that I pass on the command line as a config override. Neither alias works, although aliases in my plain user config do. Why? Explain at which points during startup the configuration is built, which facts about the environment are known at each point (repository, subcommand, directory given on the command line), how aliases and the default command are expanded, how the scoped blocks are matched, and what jj prints when the expansion would come out differently.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Aliases and the default command are expanded (expand_args: resolve_aliases, resolve_default_command, resolve_aliases again) using the config resolved at the first stage of run_internal, which has system, user, and (if the current directory is inside a workspace) repo and workspace layers, but no subcommand name and no --config layers.

CRITICAL: A scoped block conditioned on commands cannot match at that stage, because the resolution context's command is None and matches_command returns false when candidates exist but the command is unknown; the command name is only set later by ConfigEnv::set_command_name(command_name(&matches)) after clap parsing, as the space-joined subcommand chain.

Command-line --config/--config-file layers (and the color/quiet/no-pager overrides) are extracted by parse_early_args from the already expanded arguments, added to the raw config and re-resolved afterwards, so aliases inside them are not seen; warn_if_args_mismatch re-expands the arguments with the new config and prints a warning that aliases cannot be loaded from the repository path or config arguments if the result differs.

If the repository option is given, the workspace loader is recreated, the repo and workspace paths are reset and their configs reloaded, and the final resolve (applying workspace config, command-line config and the commands condition) runs only afterwards; migration of deprecated keys runs after every resolve and only the last migration messages are printed.

Matching rules in lib config_resolver: a commands entry matches if the actual command equals it or starts with it followed by a space (so 'foo' matches 'foo bar' but 'foo bar' does not match 'foo'); repositories/workspaces entries match as path prefixes of the repo path (<root>/.jj/repo) or workspace path, with a leading ~ expanded using the home directory, and fail if the path is unknown; resolve() flattens scope tables into following layers of the same source, in order.
